title: Building a Simulator

mentor.name: PHYS-1
mentor.character: Trusts nothing it cannot reproduce twice, and makes you print the difference before you claim there is one.

summary: You will build a physics simulator from the integration step up: Euler, midpoint and Runge-Kutta, collision detection, contact impulses, restitution and friction, all on a fixed timestep you control. By the end you can make a run bit for bit reproducible, record and replay it from a seed and an input tape, and measure in numbers how far your simulator sits from the machine it claims to mirror.

chapters.title: First Light in the Mirror World

lessons.title: The First Tick
lessons.goal: Write a step function that takes a state and a timestep and returns the next state.
lessons.theory:
A simulator is two things and nothing else: a **state** and a **step** function. The state is every number you need to continue from here. The step function takes that state, takes a timestep `dt`, and returns the state one `dt` later.

Everything else in this course, collision, friction, replay, is scaffolding around those two. If you can name your state and write your step, you have a simulator. If you cannot say what your state is, you do not have one, you have a loop with variables scattered through it.

The first body in The Mirror World is a 200 g test mass dropped inside a 3 metre calibration tower. Its state is two numbers: `height` in metres and `velocity` in metres per second. Gravity is a constant `GRAVITY` of -9.81 metres per second squared, negative because up is positive.

The order inside the step matters and you will spend all of chapter one on it. Today, update `velocity` from gravity, then update `height` from the velocity you just computed.
lessons.task: Fill in `step` so that it advances `velocity` with `GRAVITY` and then advances `height` with that velocity, both scaled by `dt`.
lessons.hint: Two lines. The first is velocity plus acceleration times dt, the second is height plus velocity times dt.
lessons.solution:
DT = 0.01
GRAVITY = -9.81

def step(state, dt):
    height, velocity = state
    velocity = velocity + GRAVITY * dt
    height = height + velocity * dt
    return (height, velocity)

s = (3.0, 0.0)
for i in range(5):
    s = step(s, DT)
    print(i + 1, round(s[0], 5), round(s[1], 5))

lessons.title: The Loop That Owns Time
lessons.goal: Turn a duration and a timestep into a step count and drive the state that many times.
lessons.theory:
A step function alone does not simulate anything. Something has to call it, and that something owns time.

The rule is `steps = duration / dt`, rounded to an integer because you cannot take two thirds of a step. Round it, do not truncate it: `int(0.3 / 0.1)` is 2, because 0.1 is not exactly 0.1 in binary and that division lands at 2.9999999999999996. Truncation silently drops a step and your run is short by one `dt`, every time the numbers happen to fall on the wrong side.

Notice what the loop does **not** do. It does not read a clock. It does not ask how long the last step took. The simulated world advances by exactly `dt` per call regardless of how fast or slow the machine is, and that is the property everything in chapter six depends on.

Keep `run` separate from `step`. One knows physics, the other knows time. When you later add substeps, replay and snapshots, all of it goes in `run` and none of it touches `step`.

lessons.hint: Use `int(round(duration / dt))` so that 1.0 over 0.01 is a hundred and not ninety nine.

lessons.title: The Answer You Already Know
lessons.goal: Compare the simulated height against the closed form solution and print the error.
lessons.theory:
Free fall has an exact answer written down two centuries before anyone had a computer. The height after `t` seconds is the initial height plus the initial velocity times `t` plus half of gravity times `t` squared.

That exact answer is worth more to you than any plot. It is the only way to know whether your simulator is right, and the difference between the two is the number this whole course is about. In chapter one you will make that number shrink on purpose; in chapter seven you will discover that shrinking it to zero still does not make the simulator match a real machine.

Use it wherever you can. Most systems worth simulating have no closed form, which is exactly why you simulate them, but the ones that do are your test rig. A simulator that cannot reproduce free fall to six decimals has a bug you would never find in the interesting case.

The quantity to print is `abs(sim_height - exact_height)`. Absolute, because you care how far off you are, not in which direction.

lessons.title: The World Holds a List
lessons.goal: Store several bodies in a list and advance all of them inside one step of the world.
lessons.theory:
Two loose variables were fine for one body. For three they are a mess, and for three hundred they are impossible. The state of a world is a **list of bodies**, and each body is a small mutable record.

Here each body is a list of two numbers, `[height, velocity]`. Later it grows a mass, a radius and an inverse mass, but the shape of the code never changes: `step_world` walks the list and advances every entry with the same physics.

This is also where a simulator stops looking like a physics exercise and starts looking like software. The step of the world is a loop over bodies. Everything you add after this, contacts, friction, sensors, is another loop over bodies or over pairs of them.

Use a list and not a tuple for each body, because you are going to mutate it in place. Mutating in place matters later: the contact solver writes velocities back into the same records the integrator just wrote.
lessons.task: Write `step_world(bodies, dt)` so it walks `bodies` and advances each `body` with gravity, velocity first and then height.
lessons.hint: Inside the loop, `body[1]` is the velocity and `body[0]` is the height. Write the velocity line first.

lessons.title: The Same Second, Three Step Sizes
lessons.goal: Measure how the simulated result changes when only the timestep changes.
lessons.theory:
Here is the fact that makes a simulator different from a calculation: **the answer depends on the timestep**. The same physics, the same half second, the same starting state, and three different numbers come out.

The reason is that the step function pretends the velocity is constant across the whole step, and it is not. Over a big `dt` that pretence costs a lot. Over a small one it costs little. The cost has a name, **truncation error**, and for the integrator you wrote it shrinks roughly in proportion to `dt`.

So `dt` is not a rendering detail or a performance knob. It is a physical parameter of your simulator, and quoting a result without quoting the timestep that produced it means nothing.

Run the same fall at three step sizes and print the error against `exact_height` for each. You are about to see three numbers that fall by a factor of ten each time, which is the whole of chapter one in one line of output.

lessons.title: The Spring That Gains Energy
lessons.goal: Implement explicit Euler on a mass spring and measure the energy it invents.
lessons.theory:
Free fall was forgiving because the acceleration never changed. A spring is not: the force depends on where the mass is, so the acceleration changes inside every step, and the integrator has to guess.

**Explicit Euler**, also called forward Euler, guesses with the values from the **start** of the step. It computes the next position from the current velocity and the next velocity from the current position, and neither line sees the other's result.

The test rig is a 1 kg mass on a spring of stiffness `K` of 4 newtons per metre, pulled to 1 metre and released. Total mechanical energy is `0.5 * M * v * v + 0.5 * K * x * x`, and for a real spring with no damping it is constant forever. That constant is your alarm: if the number moves, the integrator moved it, not the physics.

Run it for 20 seconds and read the two energies. Explicit Euler will hand you back more energy than you put in, which in a robot simulator means a resting arm that slowly starts to shake.
lessons.task: Fill in the step of `euler` so that `x_next` uses the current velocity and `v_next` uses the current position, both taken from the start of the step.
lessons.hint: Both right hand sides use `x` and `v`, never `x_next` or `v_next`. The spring acceleration is minus `K / M` times `x`.
lessons.starter:
M = 1.0
K = 4.0
DT = 0.01
STEPS = 2000

def energy(x, v):
    return 0.5 * M * v * v + 0.5 * K * x * x

def euler(x, v, dt, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        x_next = x
        v_next = v
        # TODO: advance both using only the values from the start of the step
        x, v = x_next, v_next
    return x, v

print("start", round(energy(1.0, 0.0), 6))
print("after 20 s", round(energy(*euler(1.0, 0.0, DT, STEPS)), 6))

    for _ in range(steps):
        x_next = x + v * dt
        v_next = v - (K / M) * x * dt

lessons.title: The Spring That Keeps It
lessons.goal: Implement semi implicit Euler and show its energy stays bounded where explicit Euler grows.
lessons.theory:
One line moved and the problem disappears. **Semi implicit Euler**, also called symplectic Euler, updates the velocity first and then moves the position with the velocity it just computed.

That is the entire change. It costs nothing, it is the same number of operations, and it turns an integrator that pumps energy into the world into one whose energy error stays inside a fixed band forever. The reason is that the update becomes a shear transformation with determinant exactly one, so it preserves area in the position and velocity plane. That is what symplectic means.

This is why almost every game physics engine and a good number of robotics simulators use it. It is not more accurate than explicit Euler step for step, and it will still drift in phase. It simply refuses to blow up, and refusing to blow up is worth more than accuracy in a simulator someone leaves running.

The code below already contains the explicit version from the last lesson. Write `symplectic` next to it and print both energies after the same 20 seconds.
lessons.task: Fill in `symplectic` so `v_next` is computed first from `x`, and `x_next` moves with `v_next` rather than with `v`.
lessons.hint: Only one symbol changes compared to `euler`: the position line reads `v_next` instead of `v`.
lessons.starter:
M = 1.0
K = 4.0
DT = 0.01
STEPS = 2000

def energy(x, v):
    return 0.5 * M * v * v + 0.5 * K * x * x

def euler(x, v, dt, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        x_next = x + v * dt
        v_next = v - (K / M) * x * dt
        x, v = x_next, v_next
    return x, v

def symplectic(x, v, dt, steps):
    for _ in range(steps):
        v_next = v
        x_next = x
        # TODO: velocity first, then move the position with the velocity you just got
        x, v = x_next, v_next
    return x, v

print("explicit", round(energy(*euler(1.0, 0.0, DT, STEPS)), 6))
print("symplectic", round(energy(*symplectic(1.0, 0.0, DT, STEPS)), 6))

DT = 0.01

    for _ in range(steps):
        x_next = x + v * dt

    return x, v

lessons.title: Halving the Step Halves the Error
lessons.goal: Measure the order of accuracy of explicit Euler by comparing errors at three step sizes.
lessons.theory:
An integrator has an **order**. It is the exponent in the relation between the timestep and the error left after a fixed amount of simulated time: halve `dt` on a first order method and the error halves, on a second order method it drops by four, on a fourth order method by sixteen.

You never have to take that on faith. Run the same simulated interval at three step sizes, compare each result against a known exact answer, and divide consecutive errors. The ratio is the number that tells you the order, and it is the single most useful measurement you can make on an integrator you did not write.

The undamped spring has an exact answer: starting at 1 metre with zero velocity, the position at time `t` is `math.cos(OMEGA * t)` with `OMEGA` equal to the square root of `K / M`, which here is 2 radians per second. Compare at `T_END`.

Expect ratios near two. Not exactly two, because the leading error term is only the first of an infinite series, and the smaller you make `dt` the closer the measured ratio creeps to the theoretical one.
lessons.task: Make `error_at` return the distance between the simulated position and `math.cos(OMEGA * T_END)`, then read the printed ratios.
lessons.hint: The exact position at the end is the cosine of `OMEGA * T_END`, and the error is the absolute difference.
lessons.starter:
import math

M = 1.0
K = 4.0
OMEGA = 2.0
T_END = 2.0

def euler_x(dt):
    x, v = 1.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(int(round(T_END / dt))):
        x, v = x + v * dt, v - (K / M) * x * dt
    return x

def error_at(dt):
    x = euler_x(dt)
    gap = abs(x)
    # TODO: measure the distance to the exact cosine solution at T_END instead
    return gap

sizes = (0.08, 0.04, 0.02)
errors = [error_at(dt) for dt in sizes]
for i in range(len(sizes)):
    print(sizes[i], round(errors[i], 8))
for i in range(len(errors) - 1):
    print("ratio", round(errors[i] / errors[i + 1], 4))

lessons.title: The Slope in the Middle
lessons.goal: Implement the midpoint method and measure that its error falls by four when the step halves.
lessons.theory:
Explicit Euler uses the slope at the start of the step for the whole step. That is why it is only first order: it is a straight line approximating a curve, anchored at the wrong end.

The **midpoint method**, the classic second order Runge-Kutta, buys a big improvement with one extra evaluation. Take a trial half step with the slope at the start, look at the slope there, then throw the trial away and take the **full** step using that middle slope. The error at the start and the error at the end cancel to first order, leaving a second order method.

In code the derivative is a separate function `deriv(x, v)` that returns the pair of rates, velocity and acceleration. Naming it separately is not decoration: every method from here on differs only in where it samples `deriv` and how it weights the samples.

The trial step is `k1x` and `k1v` scaled by `half`, which is `dt / 2.0`. The real step uses `k2x` and `k2v` scaled by the full `dt`. Watch the ratios: they should sit near four.
lessons.task: Change the second derivative sample so it is taken at the midpoint, that is at `x` plus `k1x * half` and `v` plus `k1v * half`.
lessons.hint: `deriv` is called with the trial midpoint, not with `x` and `v` again.

import math

M = 1.0
K = 4.0
OMEGA = 2.0
T_END = 2.0

def deriv(x, v):
    return v, -(K / M) * x

def midpoint_x(dt):
    x, v = 1.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(int(round(T_END / dt))):
        half = dt / 2.0
        k1x, k1v = deriv(x, v)
        k2x, k2v = deriv(x, v)
        # TODO: take the second sample at the midpoint of the trial step
        x = x + k2x * dt
        v = v + k2v * dt
    return x

errors = []
for dt in (0.08, 0.04, 0.02):
    errors.append(abs(midpoint_x(dt) - math.cos(OMEGA * T_END)))
    print(dt, round(errors[-1], 10))
for i in range(len(errors) - 1):
    print("ratio", round(errors[i] / errors[i + 1], 4))

lessons.title: Four Slopes and a Weighted Average
lessons.goal: Implement classical fourth order Runge-Kutta and measure the sixteenfold error drop.
lessons.theory:
Classical **RK4** samples the derivative four times per step: once at the start, twice at the midpoint using each previous sample as the trial, and once at the end using the third sample.

The four samples are combined with fixed weights: the step uses one sixth of `k1`, two sixths of `k2`, two sixths of `k3` and one sixth of `k4`. Written out, the combined slope is `(k1 + 2 * k2 + 2 * k3 + k4) / 6`. Those weights are not arbitrary, they are chosen so that the Taylor expansion of the numerical step matches the true solution through the fourth power of `dt`.

That is why the error drops by sixteen when the step halves, and why RK4 at a lazy step size beats Euler at a step size a thousand times smaller. It is the default integrator for anything smooth: trajectory rollouts, dynamics of an arm, aerodynamic models.

It is not the default for contact. A collision makes the derivative discontinuous inside the step, the four samples disagree about which side of the wall the body is on, and the fourth order cancellation you paid four evaluations for evaporates. That is chapter three's problem.
lessons.task: Set `wx` and `wv` to the Runge-Kutta weighted average of the four slope samples already computed above them.
lessons.hint: Each weighted slope is the first plus twice the second plus twice the third plus the fourth, all divided by six.

lessons.title: Paying in Evaluations
lessons.goal: Compare integrators at equal derivative evaluation cost instead of equal timestep.
lessons.theory:
Comparing methods at the same `dt` is comparing a bicycle to a lorry by the size of the wheels. RK4 at `dt` of 0.02 is not four times better than Euler at `dt` of 0.02, it is four times more **expensive**, because every step costs four calls to `deriv`.

In a real simulator `deriv` is the expensive part. It walks every body, sums every force, and in a robot model it may run a whole dynamics routine. The honest comparison fixes the number of derivative evaluations, calls that the `BUDGET`, and asks which method gets closest with it.

So each method gets `BUDGET // cost` steps, and its `dt` is `T_END / steps`. Euler with cost 1 gets the smallest timestep and the most steps; RK4 with cost 4 gets a quarter of the steps and a timestep four times bigger.

RK4 still wins, and it wins by orders of magnitude, because a fourth power beats a factor of four the moment `dt` is small enough. That is the real argument for higher order methods and it is a budget argument, not an elegance argument.

lessons.title: The Step That Explodes
lessons.goal: Reproduce the instability of explicit Euler on a stiff decay and find where it starts.
lessons.theory:
Accuracy is one failure mode. **Instability** is the other, and it is louder: instead of a slightly wrong answer you get a number that doubles every step until it becomes infinity.

A **stiff** system is one with a rate much faster than the interval you care about. The model here is a first order decay, `dx/dt = -LAMBDA * x` with `LAMBDA` of 100 per second, which is what a small motor's current loop or a stiff contact spring looks like from the outside. The true solution falls to nothing in about 50 ms.

Explicit Euler multiplies `x` by `(1 - LAMBDA * dt)` every step. If that factor is bigger than one in magnitude, the amplitude grows, and it does so geometrically. At `LAMBDA * dt` of 3 the factor is -2, so the answer doubles and flips sign every step.

This is not the integrator being inaccurate. Cutting the tolerance does nothing; the run is unrecoverable in a handful of steps. Print the final magnitude at four step sizes and watch where the behaviour changes.

lessons.goal: Find the stability limit of explicit Euler by scanning and check it against 2 over lambda.
lessons.theory:
The boundary you just crossed has a formula. Explicit Euler on `dx/dt = -LAMBDA * x` is stable when the magnitude of `1 - LAMBDA * dt` is at most one, which happens exactly when `dt` is at most `2 / LAMBDA`.

That is the number every stiff simulator lives under. A contact modelled as a spring of 100 kN per metre against a 1 kg body has a rate near 316 per second, so explicit Euler needs a timestep under 6 ms, and to look good rather than merely survive it needs a tenth of that. This is precisely why physics engines run at 240 Hz and above, and why a stiffer contact costs you frame rate rather than accuracy.

Do not take the formula on trust. Scan `dt` upward, run the decay at each one, and keep the `largest` value that still ends smaller than it started. Then print `limit` from the formula next to it and see whether the code agrees with the algebra.

lessons.title: The Step That Cannot Explode
lessons.goal: Implement implicit Euler for the stiff decay and show it stays bounded at any timestep.
lessons.theory:
**Implicit Euler**, or backward Euler, evaluates the derivative at the **end** of the step instead of the start. That gives `x_next = x - LAMBDA * x_next * dt`, an equation with the unknown on both sides.

For this decay you can solve it by hand: `x_next = x / (1 + LAMBDA * dt)`. The denominator is always bigger than one for positive `dt`, so the magnitude always shrinks. There is no timestep at which this blows up. You can take a half second step on a system whose natural time constant is 10 ms and still get a small, sane number back.

The price is twofold. First, it is heavily damped: it does not merely stay stable, it drains energy, and a spring integrated this way slowly dies even with no friction in the model. Second, in a general system you cannot solve for `x_next` by hand and you need a linear solve or a Newton iteration every step, which is why implicit solvers are expensive and why engines reserve them for the stiff part.

Run both at three step sizes and print them side by side. The last row is the argument in one line.

lessons.title: The Accumulator
lessons.goal: Decouple the physics timestep from the frame time with a leftover time accumulator.
lessons.theory:
The fix is to stop letting the frame decide the timestep. The physics runs at a **fixed** `FIXED_DT` forever. The frame only delivers a quantity of time into an `accumulator`, and the loop spends that time in whole fixed steps, keeping the remainder for the next frame.

A frame of 21 milliseconds with a 5 millisecond step buys four steps and leaves 1 millisecond in the accumulator. The next frame starts 1 millisecond richer. Nothing is lost and nothing is invented, so over any interval the number of physics steps depends only on how much time passed, not on how it was chopped up.

The subtraction has to be `accumulator - FIXED_DT` inside the loop, not a reset to zero. Zeroing it throws away the remainder, which is a slow leak of simulated time, and it is the most common way this pattern is written wrong.

The property to measure is sharper than it first looks. There is one **canonical** trajectory, the one produced by taking whole `FIXED_DT` steps from the start, and an accumulator run is always exactly on it: `canonical(n)` reproduces it to the last bit for whatever `n` the frames happened to buy. The frame pattern decides only how far along that timeline you have got, never which values the timeline contains. The two runs below land on step 199 and step 200 of the same line, one fixed step apart, because the frame durations do not sum to precisely one second in binary.

A variable step run has no such line to land on. Its answer is off the canonical trajectory by an amount that depends on the pattern of frames, and the last two rows measure exactly that.

lessons.title: The Frame Between Two Steps
lessons.goal: Interpolate between the last two physics states and measure the frame to frame jitter it removes.
lessons.theory:
The accumulator leaves the display in an awkward place. When a frame ends there is leftover time that has not been simulated, and how much leftover there is changes every frame. Draw the newest state as it stands and the amount of staleness jumps around, which on screen is judder even at a perfectly steady frame rate.

The standard cure keeps the state from **before** the last step as `previous` and blends it with the current one. The blend factor is `alpha`, which is `accumulator / FIXED_DT`, a number between zero and one.

Be precise about what that buys, because it is easy to claim too much. The blended point sits at exactly one `FIXED_DT` behind the frame time, always. Interpolation does **not** reduce the display lag; it adds a full step of it and makes it constant. What it removes is the variation, and the variation is the thing the eye sees.

So the honest measurement is not error against the truth, it is smoothness. The code below divides the change in displayed position by the frame duration to get an apparent velocity, compares it against the real velocity at that instant, and reports the worst disagreement. The stale display sometimes does not move at all, because that frame bought no physics step. The interpolated one is off by about one step of acceleration and never more.

lessons.title: The Spiral of Death
lessons.goal: Reproduce the runaway accumulator and stop it with a maximum frame clamp.
lessons.theory:
The accumulator has a failure mode that only appears when the machine is too slow. If one physics step costs more real time than it simulates, then every frame hands the loop more work than the work it just finished, the accumulator grows, the next frame is longer, and the loop never catches up. That is the **spiral of death**, and on screen it looks like a freeze.

Here the cost model is explicit: a step costs `COST` seconds of real time and the frame that follows lasts `OVERHEAD` plus the work the previous frame did. With `COST` above `FIXED_DT` the ratio per frame is greater than one and the frame time grows geometrically.

The cure is a ceiling. Clamp the incoming frame time to `MAX_FRAME` before it reaches the accumulator. The loop then does at most a bounded amount of work per frame and the frame time settles.

That clamp is not free and you should know what you bought. The simulated world now runs slower than the wall clock, permanently, and time that was clamped away is time the world never lived. A simulator that has to be right about how long something took must detect that condition and say so, not silently drop it.

lessons.title: Slicing the Step
lessons.goal: Split one frame into substeps and show it stabilises a contact stiff enough to blow up.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes the physics needs a smaller step than the frame rate can afford to call. A contact modelled as a spring is the standard case: a 1 kg wheel pressed onto a floor spring of `K_FLOOR` at 250 kN per metre has a natural rate of 500 radians per second, and chapter one's limit says the step has to stay under a few milliseconds or the amplitude grows.

You do not have to raise the frame rate to get that. **Substepping** takes the frame's `FIXED_DT` and divides it into `substeps` pieces of `sub_dt`, running the integrator on each. The frame rate is unchanged, the cost per frame goes up by the number of substeps, and the stability limit applies to `sub_dt` rather than to the frame.

This is the knob physics engines expose as solver substeps or position iterations. It is also the honest answer to a stack of boxes that jitters: not a better integrator, just more, smaller steps.

The contact here is preloaded, so the spring never disconnects and the run is a pure oscillator. Read the peak displacement at one, four and sixteen substeps.

lessons.title: Faster Than the World, or Slower
lessons.goal: Compute the real time factor of a run from a modelled cost per step.
lessons.theory:
A simulator has two clocks. **Simulated time** advances by `FIXED_DT` per step and is exactly what the model says. **Wall time** is what the machine spends producing it. The ratio of the first to the second is the **real time factor**, and it is the number that decides whether your simulator can sit in the loop of a real robot or only run offline.

A factor above one means the mirror world runs ahead of the real one, which is what you want for training or for batch testing. Below one means the robot would have to wait for its own model, which rules out anything in the control path.

Notice how the number is produced here. It comes from a modelled `COST_PER_STEP`, not from reading a clock. A printed wall time is different on every run and on every machine, so it cannot appear in teaching material or in a check, and chapter six explains at length why it cannot appear in a simulation either. Measure real timings when you profile; model them when you reason.

The second row multiplies the cost by ten, which is roughly what turning on a contact solver does to a scene full of bodies. Watch the factor cross one.

lessons.title: Landing Exactly on the Event
lessons.goal: Split a step at the exact time of an event and measure the error the unsplit version leaves.
lessons.theory:
Events do not respect your timestep. A command arrives at 37 milliseconds, a limit switch closes, a thruster fires. The loop only knows about instants that are multiples of `FIXED_DT`, so the naive answer applies the event at a boundary and is wrong by up to a whole step.

The cure is to split the step. When `EVENT_TIME` falls inside the interval you are about to integrate, advance by `before`, which is the time from now to the event, apply the change, then advance by the rest of the step. The world lands on the event exactly.

The integrator here carries the `0.5 * a * dt * dt` term, so it is exact for a piecewise constant acceleration. That means the split run should reproduce the closed form answer to the last digit and the unsplit one should not, and the difference between the two printed errors is purely the cost of quantising the event.

This is the same machinery a collision needs. Chapter three finds the exact time a body crosses a wall inside a step, and then this is what it does with it.

lessons.hint: The event is `EVENT_TIME` and the step starts at `t`, so the first slice is the difference between them.

EVENT_TIME = 0.037
FIXED_DT = 0.01
ACCEL = 6.0
DURATION = 0.1

def advance(x, v, a, dt):
    x = x + v * dt + 0.5 * a * dt * dt
    v = v + a * dt
    return x, v

def run(split):
    x, v, t, a = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(int(round(DURATION / FIXED_DT))):
        if split and t < EVENT_TIME < t + FIXED_DT:
            before = 0.0
            # TODO: make the first slice reach exactly to the event
            x, v = advance(x, v, a, before)
            a = ACCEL
            x, v = advance(x, v, a, FIXED_DT - before)
        else:
            if t + FIXED_DT > EVENT_TIME:
                a = ACCEL
            x, v = advance(x, v, a, FIXED_DT)
        t = t + FIXED_DT
    return x

truth = 0.5 * ACCEL * (DURATION - EVENT_TIME) * (DURATION - EVENT_TIME)
print("closed form", round(truth, 8))
print("split step error", round(abs(run(True) - truth), 8))
print("whole step error", round(abs(run(False) - truth), 8))

lessons.title: The Order Inside the Step
lessons.goal: Measure the penetration caused by resolving contacts before integrating instead of after.
lessons.theory:
A step is not one operation, it is a sequence, and the sequence is part of the model. Read inputs, apply forces, integrate, resolve contacts, advance the clock. Swap two of those and the world changes.

The expensive mistake is resolving contacts **before** integrating. The solver looks at the state, finds nothing overlapping, declares the world clean, and then the integrator drives the body straight through the floor and leaves it there until the next frame. Every frame the body spends one full step of motion below the surface.

Do it the other way and the contact solver sees exactly what the integrator produced, so nothing is ever left overlapping when the step returns. That is the invariant worth defending: **when a step ends, the world is legal**.

The two runs below use the same integrator, the same clamp and the same number of steps. The only difference is the order, and the number printed is the deepest the body ever got below the floor.
lessons.task: Write both orders: one resolving before integrating, one integrating before resolving, and print the worst penetration each produces.
lessons.hint: Nest the calls: one line is `integrate(resolve(...))` and the other is `resolve(integrate(...))`.

The counter is not redundant with the time: `self.steps` is an integer that is always exact, while `self.time` is a float that has been added to thousands of times, and chapter six measures how far apart those two drift.

lessons.title: The Floor Is a Half Space
lessons.goal: Compute the signed distance from a point to a plane and read its sign as inside or outside.
lessons.theory:
The cheapest collision shape in any simulator is a **plane**, written as a unit normal and an offset. Everything on the side the normal points to is legal, everything behind it is inside the wall. Floors, walls and the ground under a rover are all half spaces.

The test is one dot product. For a point and a plane whose unit normal is `(nx, ny)` and whose offset from the origin is `offset`, the **signed distance** is `nx * px + ny * py - offset`. The sign and the magnitude both matter. Every contact solver in the next chapter needs the depth, not just a yes or no, because how hard it pushes back depends on how far in the body got.

The normal must be **unit length**. If it is not, the number you get back is scaled by the length of the normal and is no longer a distance in metres, which is the classic way this test silently returns a depth that is 40 percent too small.

lessons.theory:
A circle against a circle is the test every two dimensional engine leans on, and a sphere against a sphere is its three dimensional twin. Both come down to one comparison: the `distance` between centres against the sum of the radii.

What the solver needs is not the boolean. It needs the **depth**, which is `ra + rb - distance`, positive when they overlap, and the **normal**, which is the unit vector along the line of centres. Divide the centre difference by the distance and you have it.

The division is the trap. Two bodies exactly on top of each other give a distance of zero and the normal is genuinely undefined, so the code has to pick one rather than raise. That case is not theoretical: bodies spawned at the same point, or a stack that has been squeezed flat by a bad solver, hit it in the first second of a run. The guard is already written for you below.

This is also the cheapest shape to reason about mass and inertia for, which is why rovers, wheels and grippers get approximated as discs long before anyone reaches for a mesh.

lessons.title: Boxes That Do Not Turn
lessons.goal: Test two axis aligned boxes for overlap by measuring the overlap of their intervals on each axis.
lessons.theory:
An **axis aligned bounding box** is a box that never rotates. It is the second cheapest shape after the plane and the standard stand in for anything complicated, because two of them overlap only if their intervals overlap on **every** axis.

So the whole test reduces to a one dimensional question asked twice. Two intervals overlap by `min(a_max, b_max) - max(a_min, b_min)`, and that expression is worth memorising: positive is the overlap in metres, negative is the gap in metres, and it never needs a branch.

The axis with the **smaller** overlap is the one to push along, because it is the shortest way out. That is the minimum translation vector, and for axis aligned boxes it is free: you already computed both numbers.

This test is what almost every broad phase runs first, even for round or irregular bodies, because a box around a shape is cheap to build and rejecting a pair here saves the expensive test entirely.

lessons.title: Every Pair Is Too Many
lessons.goal: Cut the number of candidate pairs with a uniform grid and prove it misses no real overlap.
lessons.theory:
Testing every body against every other body costs `n * (n - 1) / 2` pairs. At a hundred bodies that is 4.950 tests per step, at a thousand it is half a million, and the narrow phase test is the expensive part. This is the **broad phase** problem and it is why large scenes need a spatial structure.

The simplest one that works is a uniform grid. Drop each body into the cell its centre falls in, using `int(x // CELL)` and `int(y // CELL)` as the key, and only test bodies in the same cell or in the eight around it.

That neighbourhood is only sufficient if `CELL` is at least as large as the biggest body diameter. Below that, two bodies can overlap while sitting two cells apart and the grid quietly loses the contact. Here the largest body is 0,2 metres across and `CELL` is 0,25, so the condition holds.

A broad phase is only allowed to add candidates, never to remove real contacts. That is why the last line does not just report a smaller number: it recomputes the true overlaps by brute force and counts how many the grid failed to offer. Any answer other than zero means the acceleration structure is a bug, not an optimisation.

lessons.theory:
A range sensor in a simulator is a **ray cast**: an origin, a direction, and the question of what it hits first. The same routine serves for a lidar beam, a line of sight check and a bullet.

Against a circle the algebra is a quadratic. Write the ray as origin plus `t` times direction, substitute it into the circle equation, and you get `a * t * t + b * t + c = 0` with `a` from the direction, `b` from the direction against the offset from the centre, and `c` from that offset against the radius. Those three are already computed below.

The **discriminant** `disc` is `b * b - 4.0 * a * c`. Negative means the line misses entirely. Zero or positive means it crosses, and the nearer crossing is the root with the minus sign, `(-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2.0 * a)`.

One more check belongs in real code: a negative `t` means the circle is **behind** the sensor, which for a lidar is not a hit at all. Chapter nine puts that check in when the beam becomes a sensor model with a maximum range.

lessons.goal: Reproduce tunnelling by testing for overlap only at the end of each step.

Every test in this chapter so far asks the same question: are these two shapes overlapping **right now**. That question is asked once per step, at the end of it, and between two of those instants the body is not observed at all.

A projectile at 500 metres per second with a 4 millisecond step moves 2 metres per step. A wall 5 centimetres thick occupies 5 centimetres of that 2 metre jump. The body is in front of the wall at the end of one step and behind it at the end of the next, and the discrete test never sees an overlap. The failure is not a bug in the overlap test. The test is correct at every instant it is asked. The bug is that the model only exists at instants, and the wall is thinner than the distance between them.

That gives the rule of thumb: a discrete engine is safe while the fastest body moves less than the thinnest obstacle per step. The four step sizes below cross that boundary. Read where the hits appear.

lessons.title: Sweeping the Step
lessons.goal: Find the fraction of the step at which the body crosses the wall face and catch every crossing.
lessons.theory:
The cure for tunnelling is to stop asking about instants and start asking about the **segment** the body swept during the step. That is **continuous collision detection**.

For a body moving in a straight line against a plane the answer is one division. If the body starts the step at `x` and would end it at `x_next`, the fraction of the step at which it reaches the face is `toi = (WALL_MIN - x) / (x_next - x)`. A value between zero and one means the crossing happened inside this step, whatever the step size was.

That name, **time of impact**, is what you feed to the machinery of lesson sm2-7: advance to `toi`, apply the contact, then finish the rest of the step. The two pieces were built separately and they fit together here.

Continuous detection is not free, so engines apply it selectively: a flag per body, usually called bullet or continuous, turned on for projectiles and fast wheels and left off for the crates. The run below prints the discrete count next to the swept one at every step size, and the swept column should not care.

lessons.title: What a Contact Carries
lessons.goal: Package a detected overlap into a contact record with normal, depth and point.
lessons.theory:
Detection and response are separate stages, and the thing that crosses between them is the **contact record**. Getting its contents right is what lets the solver in the next chapter stay short.

A contact carries four things. Which two bodies are involved, so the solver knows whose velocities to touch. The unit **normal**, the direction the push has to act along. The **depth**, how far they interpenetrate. And the **point**, where on the surface it happened, which matters the moment bodies can rotate.

Conventions have to be fixed once and never argued with again. Here the normal always points from body `a` towards body `b`, depth is positive when overlapping, and a static body is written as index -1. A solver that has to ask which way a normal points is a solver with a sign bug waiting in it.

Returning `None` for no contact is deliberate. The alternative, a record with zero depth, means the solver runs its whole path for pairs that are not touching, and zero depth contacts are exactly the ones that produce jitter.

lessons.title: Two Boxes That Turn
lessons.goal: Detect overlap between convex polygons with the separating axis test and return the shortest push.
lessons.theory:
The moment a box is allowed to rotate the axis aligned test is useless. The general answer for convex shapes is the **separating axis theorem**: two convex polygons are apart if and only if there exists a line onto which their projections do not overlap, and it is enough to check the normals of their edges.

So the algorithm is a loop over every edge of both polygons. Build the edge normal, project both polygons onto it with a dot product, and measure the overlap of the two intervals with the same expression from lesson sm3-3.

Two outcomes matter. If any axis gives an overlap at or below zero, the shapes are apart and you can stop immediately, which is what makes this test fast in the common case. If every axis overlaps, the shapes intersect and the axis with the **smallest** overlap is the minimum translation vector, the shortest direction and distance that separates them.

Normalising each axis is not optional. Without it the overlaps are measured in different units on each axis and the smallest one is not the shortest push, only the one whose edge happened to be longest. That bug produces boxes that pop sideways instead of up.

        lx, ly = sx * hw, sy * hh
        corners.append((cx + lx * math.cos(angle) - ly * math.sin(angle),
                        cy + lx * math.sin(angle) + ly * math.cos(angle)))

def sat(pa, pb):
    best = 1e9
    bx, by = 0.0, 0.0
    for poly in (pa, pb):
        for i in range(len(poly)):

lessons.title: Pushing It Out
lessons.goal: Remove penetration with a positional correction along the contact normal.
lessons.theory:
Detection tells you a body is 3 millimetres inside the floor. Response has to do something about it, and the first thing it does is put the body back where it belongs.

**Positional correction** moves the body along the contact normal by the penetration depth, so that the surfaces touch exactly. It is not physics, it is bookkeeping: nothing in the world applies a force that teleports a wheel 3 millimetres. What it does is defend the invariant from lesson sm2-8, that when a step ends the world is legal.

The inward part of the velocity has to go too. Leave it and the next step drives the body straight back in, the correction fires again, and you have built a body that hovers while consuming solver time forever.

Run the same fall twice, once with the correction and once without. The uncorrected body does not stop at the floor, it does not even slow down: nothing in the integrator knows the floor exists.

lessons.title: The Bounce Coefficient
lessons.goal: Reflect the normal velocity scaled by a restitution coefficient and watch the bounces decay.
lessons.theory:
A body that stops dead at every contact is a body made of clay. Real contacts give some of the approach speed back, and the fraction they return is the **coefficient of restitution**, written `e` and living between 0 and 1.

At `e` of 1 the collision is perfectly elastic and nothing is lost. At 0 the body sticks, which is the clay from lesson sm4-1. A steel ball bearing on a granite slab is around 0.95, a rubber tyre on concrete around 0.6, a robot chassis landing on a rubber mat around 0.2. Those numbers are properties of the **pair** of materials, not of one of them, which is why a real engine stores a restitution table and not a field per body.

The rule is one line: the outgoing normal velocity is minus `RESTITUTION` times the incoming normal velocity. Only the normal component is touched. The tangential component is friction's business and that is the next chapter.

The apex height is not proportional to `e`, it is proportional to `e` squared, and knowing which one saves an afternoon of confusion when a bounce looks too dead.

lessons.theory:
A geometric sequence never reaches zero. In the model the ball bounces forever, each bounce shorter than the last, and once the bounces are smaller than a timestep the simulator is spending a contact solve per step on motion nobody can see.

That is where resting jitter comes from, and it is expensive: contacts that never go away, solver iterations that never converge, and a body that visibly shivers on the floor.

Every engine cuts it the same way. Below a **restitution velocity threshold**, typically around 1 metre per second in a game and much smaller in a robotics simulator, the restitution is forced to zero and the contact becomes perfectly inelastic. The ball stops instead of bouncing 4 microns.

It is an approximation and it should be an explicit one. If your simulation is about how a part settles in a feeder, `REST_SPEED` is a parameter of your model with an effect on the answer, and it belongs in the report next to the restitution. The run counts real bounces, that is contacts that left with an upward velocity, over the last stretch of the run.

lessons.goal: Resolve a collision between two moving bodies with a single impulse and check momentum is conserved.
lessons.theory:
So far one side of every contact has been a wall that does not care. Two moving bodies need an **impulse**, a single number applied equally and oppositely along the normal, which is the discrete version of a force acting for an instant.

The magnitude comes straight out of the restitution law and conservation of momentum: `j = -(1.0 + restitution) * v_rel / (inv_a + inv_b)`, where `v_rel` is the relative velocity along the normal and `inv_a` and `inv_b` are the inverse masses. Body a gets `j * inv_a` subtracted, body b gets `j * inv_b` added.

Working in **inverse mass** rather than mass is not a micro optimisation. It removes a division from the inner loop, and it makes an immovable body expressible as a plain zero, which is the whole of the next lesson.

Momentum conservation is the test that catches sign errors here, because it holds no matter what the restitution is: whatever one body gains the other loses, exactly. If the printed total moves, the impulse is not being applied symmetrically and everything built on top of it will drift.

lessons.goal: Represent an immovable body as a zero inverse mass and show the impulse leaves it untouched.
lessons.theory:
A wall, a floor and a table are bodies with infinite mass. Infinity is awkward in code: it propagates through arithmetic, it turns divisions into zero and subtractions into `nan`, and it makes every formula need a special case.

Working in inverse mass makes the problem disappear. Infinite mass is inverse mass **zero**, a perfectly ordinary float. The impulse formula from the previous lesson then does the right thing with no branch: the denominator only counts the movable bodies, and the immovable one has its velocity change multiplied by zero.

The convention used here is that a mass of zero or less means immovable, so `inv = 0.0 if mass <= 0.0 else 1.0 / mass`. That inversion between the stored value and its meaning is standard and it catches people out, so name the field `inv_mass` and never store a mass at all.

One guard is still required. If both bodies are immovable the denominator is zero and the division raises. Two static bodies should never generate a contact in the first place, but a broad phase that files the floor in a cell will hand you that pair on the first frame, so the check belongs in the solver.
lessons.task: Fill in `inverse_mass` with the convention above and confirm the wall keeps its velocity while the ball reverses.
lessons.hint: A conditional expression: zero when the mass is not positive, otherwise one over the mass.

    inv = 1.0
    # TODO: turn a mass into an inverse mass, treating a non positive mass as immovable
    return inv

def collide(inv_a, va, inv_b, vb, restitution):
    if inv_a + inv_b <= 0.0:
        return va, vb
    v_rel = vb - va
    j = -(1.0 + restitution) * v_rel / (inv_a + inv_b)
    return va - j * inv_a, vb + j * inv_b

lessons.title: The Correction That Launches
lessons.goal: Damp the penetration feedback with slop and bias and measure the extra bounce height it removes.
lessons.theory:
Lesson sm4-1 removed penetration by teleporting the body. Production solvers do not teleport, they add a **bias velocity**: an extra outgoing speed proportional to how deep the body got, so the penetration is worked off through the same normal velocity path as everything else.

The naive version asks for all of it back in one step, which is `depth / DT`. That is a speed, and for a fast impact it is a large one. A body arriving at 2,4 metres per second with a 5 millisecond step can be 12 millimetres inside the floor before the contact is noticed, and 12 millimetres over 5 milliseconds is 2,4 metres per second handed straight back. The body leaves faster than it arrived. That is the **pop**, and it is why an object dropped in a badly tuned engine can bounce higher than it started.

The cure is the two constants every solver carries. Forgive `SLOP` metres of penetration entirely, and feed back only `BIAS` of what is left, so the correction becomes `max(depth - SLOP, 0.0) * BIAS / DT`. Typical values are a slop of a few millimetres and a bias between 0,1 and 0,4.

One drop is not enough to measure this, and that matters more than it looks. How deep the body gets depends on where the impact falls relative to the step grid, so a single height can land a hair past the surface and show almost no pop at all. The run scans five drop heights, divides each measured apex by what the restitution predicts, and reports the worst case. A fixture whose verdict depends on where the grid happened to fall is not a fixture.
lessons.task: Build the damped `push` from `depth`, `SLOP`, `BIAS` and `DT`, then read the worst apex ratio each version produces across the five drops.
lessons.hint: Subtract the slop, clamp at zero, scale by the bias, and divide by the timestep to turn it back into a speed.
lessons.starter:
GRAVITY = -9.81
DT = 0.005
RADIUS = 0.1
RESTITUTION = 0.5
SLOP = 0.005
BIAS = 0.1

def first_apex(drop, damped):
    y, v = drop, 0.0
    bounced = False
    for _ in range(4000):
        previous = v
        v = v + GRAVITY * DT
        y = y + v * DT
        depth = RADIUS - y
        if depth > 0.0:
            y = RADIUS
            push = depth / DT
            if damped:
                push = depth / DT
                # TODO: forgive SLOP of penetration and feed back only BIAS of the rest
            v = -RESTITUTION * v + push
            bounced = True
        if bounced and previous > 0.0 and v <= 0.0:
            return y - RADIUS
    return y - RADIUS

worst_hard = 0.0
worst_damped = 0.0
for drop in (0.4, 0.55, 0.7, 0.85, 1.0):
    predicted = RESTITUTION * RESTITUTION * (drop - RADIUS)
    hard = first_apex(drop, False) / predicted
    damped = first_apex(drop, True) / predicted
    worst_hard = max(worst_hard, hard)
    worst_damped = max(worst_damped, damped)
    print("drop", drop, "hard", round(hard, 3), "damped", round(damped, 3))
print("worst hard bias", round(worst_hard, 3))
print("worst slop and bias", round(worst_damped, 3))

lessons.title: A Stack Needs Repeats
lessons.goal: Run the contact solver several times per step and measure how the stack penetration falls with iterations.
lessons.theory:
A single body against the floor is solved by one pass. A stack is not, and the reason is that the contacts are **coupled**: fixing the contact between the second and third crate moves the second crate, which breaks the contact between the first and second that you just fixed.

The standard answer is not a better equation, it is repetition. Solve the contacts one after another, in a fixed order, and then do it again. This is Gauss-Seidel, and each pass propagates the correction one contact further up the stack. Engines expose it as solver iterations or position iterations, and 4 to 10 is the usual range.

Repetition converges but never finishes. A tall stack with a low iteration count sags visibly, and the sag is not a bug you can remove, it is the residual of an iterative method stopped early.

The order is part of the answer too. Solving bottom up propagates support upward in a single pass and looks almost solved; solving top down needs as many passes as the stack is tall. The solver below runs top down on purpose, so the effect of the iteration count is visible instead of hidden.
lessons.task: Run `solve_contacts` the requested number of times per step, and read the worst penetration left at one, four and sixteen iterations.
lessons.hint: Wrap the single call in a loop over `iterations`.

lessons.title: Inside the Cone
lessons.goal: Clamp a tangential impulse to the Coulomb friction limit set by the normal impulse.
lessons.theory:
Friction in a solver is not a force you add, it is a **limit you enforce**. The tangential impulse you would like to apply is whatever stops the sliding dead. The one you are allowed to apply is at most `MU` times the normal impulse of that same contact.

That is Coulomb's law written the way an impulse solver needs it: `limit = MU * normal_impulse`, and the applied value is the wanted one clamped into the interval from minus limit to plus limit. Drawn in three dimensions the allowed impulses form a cone around the normal, which is why this is called the friction cone.

The consequence is the useful part. When the wanted impulse fits inside the limit the surfaces stick and the sliding stops completely within the step. When it does not, the contact slides and the friction only removes what the limit allows. One clamp gives you both regimes with no branch and no state.

Notice that the limit depends on the normal impulse of **this** step. A body pressed hard has more grip, a body barely touching has almost none, and a body in free fall for one step has a normal impulse of zero and therefore no friction at all. That coupling is what makes a wheel lose grip over a bump.
lessons.task: Set `limit` from `MU` and the normal impulse, and clamp `wanted` into it to get `applied`.
lessons.hint: The clamp is `max(-limit, min(limit, wanted))`.

    wanted = -tangent_speed * MASS
    limit = 1e9
    applied = wanted
    # TODO: build the Coulomb limit for this contact and clamp the wanted impulse into it
    return wanted, limit, applied

cases = (("light touch", 1.5, 0.4), ("firm contact", 1.5, 12.0), ("crawling", 0.05, 12.0))

lessons.title: Static Beats Kinetic
lessons.goal: Switch between a static and a kinetic coefficient using a sticking speed threshold.
lessons.theory:
One coefficient is a simplification. Surfaces at rest interlock, and it takes more force to start them moving than to keep them moving. `MU_STATIC` is typically 20 to 50 percent above `MU_KINETIC` for dry contacts, and the gap is what makes a heavy crate lurch when you finally shift it.

A solver cannot ask whether the contact is at rest, because in a floating point world it never is exactly. It asks whether the sliding speed is below a threshold, `STICK_SPEED`, and picks the coefficient from that. The threshold is a modelling parameter and it belongs in the report: too small and nothing ever sticks, too large and a genuinely sliding contact gets more grip than it should.

The useful number for a real robot is the **breakaway force**, the static coefficient times the normal load. That is the force a drive has to produce before anything moves at all, and it is the reason a gearmotor sized on the rolling load stalls at the first attempt to start on a rough floor.

Getting this wrong in a simulator is one of the sharpest sources of the reality gap in chapter seven: a model with a single coefficient predicts a robot that always starts moving, and the real one sometimes does not.

lessons.title: The Slope That Decides
lessons.goal: Find the angle at which a block starts to slide and check it against the arctangent of the coefficient.
lessons.theory:
A block on an incline is held by friction until the component of gravity along the slope beats the friction limit. Write both sides out and the mass cancels, the gravity cancels, and what is left is astonishingly simple: the block slides when `math.tan(angle) > mu`.

So the critical angle is `math.atan(mu)` and nothing else. A 40 kilogram robot and a 40 gram bolt made of the same materials slide at the same angle. This is the **angle of repose**, and it is how coefficients are measured in practice: tilt a plank until the sample moves and read the protractor.

For a robot it is a ramp specification. Rubber on dry concrete gives a coefficient near 0,7, which is 35 degrees, and a wheel on wet steel plate gives 0,2, which is 11. Any ramp steeper than that is not a traction problem you can solve with a bigger motor.

The scan below steps the angle by one milliradian, so the measured answer can only ever be within a milliradian of the truth, and quoting it to more digits than that would be inventing precision. Read the two columns and check they agree to that resolution.

lessons.title: Dry and Wet
lessons.goal: Compare Coulomb friction against viscous damping and show only one of them ever stops the body.
lessons.theory:
There are two ways to slow something down and they behave nothing alike.

**Dry** friction, the Coulomb kind, has a magnitude that does not depend on the speed at all: `-MU * NORMAL_FORCE` in the direction opposing motion. The deceleration is constant, so the speed falls along a straight line and reaches zero at a definite time, at a definite distance.

**Viscous** damping is proportional to speed, `-DAMPING * velocity`. The slower the body goes the less it is slowed, so the speed decays exponentially and never actually reaches zero. It is what a fluid, an air gap or a back electromotive force does.

Simulators reach for viscous damping because it is stable and cheap, and then people are surprised when a model of a bearing never comes to rest and the solver spends the rest of the run on a body that is moving at ten nanometres per second. If your thing stops, model dry friction and include the stop condition, because the flat portion of the curve is exactly the part viscous damping cannot produce. The two numbers below are the whole argument.

lessons.hint: `math.copysign(1.0, velocity)` gives the direction, and viscous damping needs no sign because the velocity carries it.

lessons.title: Stick and Slip
lessons.goal: Reproduce the stick slip lurch and measure the peak speed the coefficient gap produces.
lessons.theory:
Drag something slowly through a spring over a surface where sticking grips harder than sliding, and the motion is not smooth. It sticks while the spring winds up, breaks away when the spring beats the static limit, shoots forward because the sliding friction is suddenly lower, then stops and sticks again.

That is **stick slip**, and it is the noise a door hinge makes, the chatter of a robot joint under a low speed command, and the reason a cheap linear stage cannot hold a smooth 1 millimetre per second feed.

The signature is not how often the block moves, it is **how fast it moves when it does**. Both runs below break away many times, because a discrete solver re sticks whenever the velocity crosses zero. What separates them is the peak: with equal coefficients the block creeps along at roughly the speed it is being pulled, and with a gap of 0,25 it lurches at more than twenty times that. Reading the count alone would have told you the opposite of the truth, which is why the run prints the ratio.

The cause is exact. At breakaway the spring is holding `mu_static` times the load and the friction drops immediately to `MU_KINETIC` times it, so the block is left with the difference as net force. Make the two coefficients equal and that difference is zero, and no amount of tuning the spring or the pull speed brings the lurch back.
lessons.task: Break the block away when the spring force beats the static limit, counting each slip, and compare the peak speed of the two coefficient pairs.
lessons.hint: Compare `spring_force` against `mu_static * NORMAL_FORCE`, clear the stuck flag and add one to the counter.

BLOCK_MASS = 1.0
K_SPRING = 40.0
PULL_SPEED = 0.02
NORMAL_FORCE = BLOCK_MASS * 9.81
MU_KINETIC = 0.35
DT = 0.0005

def drag(mu_static):
    anchor = 0.0
    x = 0.0
    v = 0.0
    stuck = True
    slips = 0
    peak = 0.0
    for _ in range(60000):
        anchor = anchor + PULL_SPEED * DT
        spring_force = K_SPRING * (anchor - x)
        if stuck:
            v = 0.0
            # TODO: break away once the spring beats the static limit, and count that slip
        else:
            friction = -MU_KINETIC * NORMAL_FORCE * math.copysign(1.0, v)
            v = v + (spring_force + friction) / BLOCK_MASS * DT
            x = x + v * DT
            peak = max(peak, v)
            if v <= 0.0:
                v = 0.0
                stuck = True
    return slips, peak, x

for mu_static in (0.35, 0.6):
    slips, peak, x = drag(mu_static)
    print("static", mu_static, "kinetic", MU_KINETIC, "slips", slips,
          "peak speed", round(peak, 5), "times the pull", round(peak / PULL_SPEED, 2))

lessons.title: Friction Inside the Contact Solver
lessons.goal: Apply a clamped tangential impulse alongside the normal impulse and measure the sliding distance it removes.
lessons.theory:
Everything so far treated friction as a force computed on its own. Inside a real solver it is not: it is a second impulse applied at the same contact, in the same step, using the normal impulse that contact just produced.

The order is fixed. Resolve the normal direction first, because the friction limit depends on its result. Then compute the tangential impulse that would stop the sliding, `-MASS * vx`, clamp it into the cone, and apply it.

Once the body is resting, the normal impulse per step is only what gravity added during that step, `MASS * GRAVITY * DT`. So the friction budget per step is small, and the body decelerates at `MU * GRAVITY` regardless of the timestep. That is the correct answer: the deceleration of a sliding body does not depend on how finely you chop time, and if yours does, the friction is being applied without reference to the normal impulse.

The two runs below differ by that one clamp. The one without it slides forever, because nothing in the model has any opinion about the tangential direction at all.

lessons.title: The Wheel That Resists Rolling
lessons.goal: Model rolling resistance and check the coasting distance against the closed form.
lessons.theory:
A wheel that rolls without sliding still loses energy. The tyre deforms at the front of the contact patch and recovers at the back, and the recovery gives back less than the deformation took. The standard model wraps all of that into one dimensionless number, the **coefficient of rolling resistance**, and the resisting force is that coefficient times the normal load.

It is much smaller than sliding friction and it is the number that decides how far a robot coasts and how long its battery lasts. Hard rubber on smooth concrete is around 0,012, a pneumatic tyre on tarmac around 0,015, the same tyre on cut grass around 0,06, and a tracked base on gravel is several times worse.

Because the resisting force is constant in magnitude, the closed form is the same shape as dry friction: the coasting distance is `v0 * v0 / (2.0 * crr * G)`. That gives you a check you can run against a real robot with a tape measure and a stopwatch, which makes it one of the few simulator parameters you can calibrate in an afternoon.

Read the two rows. The same push carries the rover four times further on concrete than on grass, and the simulated distance should sit on the formula to within a step of integration error.

lessons.title: The Tyre That Spins
lessons.goal: Model traction as a function of slip ratio and show a command past the grip limit produces spin instead of speed.
lessons.theory:
A wheel and the ground it touches do not move at the same speed. The difference, normalised, is the **slip ratio**: `slip = (wheel - ground) / max(abs(wheel), EPS)`, zero when the wheel rolls perfectly and one when it spins on a stationary robot.

Grip is a function of that number, not of the torque you asked for. The standard curve rises steeply from zero, peaks at a small slip, `SLIP_PEAK` here, and then falls away. Modelled linearly up to the peak it is `grip = MU_PEAK * min(abs(slip) / SLIP_PEAK, 1.0)`, and the force on the body is that grip times the normal load.

The consequence is the point of the lesson. Beyond the peak, asking the wheel to turn faster does not accelerate the robot at all, it only raises the slip. The body's acceleration is capped at `MU_PEAK * G` no matter what the drive does, so the difference between a modest command and an absurd one is entirely wheel spin.

A simulator without a slip model will happily report that the rover reaches the commanded speed instantly, and a controller tuned against that model will floor the wheels on the first hill. The three rows below are the same robot with three commands.

lessons.title: The Air Pushes Back
lessons.goal: Add quadratic aerodynamic drag and check the simulated terminal speed against the closed form.
lessons.theory:
Above walking pace, air resistance stops being a rounding error. The standard model is quadratic: `drag = -0.5 * RHO * CD * AREA * velocity * abs(velocity)`, with `RHO` the air density at 1,225 kilograms per cubic metre at sea level, `CD` a shape coefficient, and `AREA` the frontal area.

Writing it as `velocity * abs(velocity)` rather than `velocity * velocity` is not a stylistic choice. The squared form loses the sign, so the drag on a falling body points down and the simulation accelerates without limit. That sign bug is quiet: it looks correct for anything moving in the positive direction and only shows up when something reverses.

Quadratic drag gives a **terminal velocity**, the speed where drag exactly cancels weight: `terminal = math.sqrt(2.0 * MASS * G / (RHO * CD * AREA))`. It is the only closed form in this chapter that is easy to check, and it is a good sanity test on any drag model you inherit.

For a small quadrotor this matters directly. A 0,8 kilogram airframe with 500 square centimetres of frontal area and a coefficient near 1,1 terminates around 15 metres per second, which is well inside the speed range it flies at, so a simulator that omits drag will overstate its descent rate and understate the power it needs to hold position in wind.

lessons.title: Two Seeds, One Program
lessons.goal: Seed the generator per run so the same seed reproduces a run exactly and a different seed does not.
lessons.theory:
A simulator that gives a different answer every time it runs is not a measuring instrument, it is a slot machine. You cannot bisect a bug in it, you cannot compare two controllers with it, and you cannot file a report anyone else can open.

Randomness is not the problem. Noise, disturbances and randomised parameters are all legitimate parts of a model. The problem is randomness you cannot **reproduce**, which is what an unseeded generator gives you. The starting code below deliberately shares one unseeded generator between runs, so pressing run twice prints two different numbers. That is the defect this whole chapter exists to remove.

The fix is one line and it is the same line in every language: give each run its own generator, constructed from a seed the run was handed. Never call the module level `random.random`, never let a library reach for the global generator, and pass the seed explicitly rather than setting it once at the top, because a single global seed makes the answer depend on the order in which parts of the program happened to ask for numbers.

Notice what the run below proves and how. It never compares its output against a previous run of the program, because that comparison cannot be printed. It compares two runs **against each other, inside the same program**, and prints the difference. That is the only way to demonstrate reproducibility in output that has to be identical every time.
lessons.task: Give `run` its own generator seeded from `seed`, then read the difference between two runs with the same seed and between two runs with different ones.
lessons.hint: `random.Random(seed)` builds an independent generator whose sequence depends only on that seed.

        x = x + v * DT

lessons.title: The Order of the Pairs
lessons.goal: Show that summing the same contact impulses in a different order changes the answer, and fix it with a canonical order.
lessons.theory:
Seeding the generator is the easy half. The harder half is that floating point addition is **not associative**, so the same set of numbers added in a different order gives a different answer.

That matters because a contact solver adds up impulses, and the order it adds them in comes from whatever the broad phase produced. Change the insertion order of a dictionary, iterate a set, run the pairs across threads, and the sums land on different last bits. Nothing is wrong with any of the numbers. The run is simply not the same run.

The cure is a **canonical order**. Sort the pairs by a stable identifier before you consume them, so the sequence of additions is a function of the contents and not of how they arrived. Body identifiers are integers assigned in creation order, and that is exactly what they are for.

The run below sums the same sixty impulses twice, once in insertion order and once shuffled with a seeded shuffle, and prints the difference. It then does the same through the canonical sum. The first difference is small. Small is not zero, and a difference of one part in 10 to the 16 is enough to send the run in lesson sm6-6 somewhere else entirely.

lessons.title: Addition Is Not Associative
lessons.goal: Measure the difference between summing the same list forwards and backwards.
lessons.theory:
The previous lesson used the fact. This one measures it, because the size of the effect decides how much it should worry you.

A float has 53 bits of mantissa. Adding a small number to a large one rounds the small one away, so the answer depends on how large the running total was at the moment each term arrived. The classic three number case is in the starting code: `(1e16 + -1e16) + 1.0` is 1,0 and `1e16 + (-1e16 + 1.0)` is 0,0, and both are the correct rounded answer to the sum they were asked to compute.

At the scale of a simulator the terms are not that extreme, but the list is long. Two hundred impulses spanning eight orders of magnitude, summed forwards and backwards, disagree in the last few bits, and that disagreement is what you are hunting when a replay goes off the rails.

The way out is not to fear floats. It is to make the order of operations part of the specification: fixed iteration order, fixed grouping, no reductions whose order the runtime is free to choose. Then the arithmetic is as reproducible as integer arithmetic, even though it is still inexact.

lessons.title: The Clock That Drifts
lessons.goal: Compare an accumulated simulation clock against one computed from the step index and find where they part.
lessons.theory:
Lesson sm2-9 gave the world both a `time` and a `steps` counter and promised this measurement. Here it is.

Accumulating `time = time + DT` performs one rounding per step, and the roundings do not cancel. Computing the same instant as `(i + 1) * DT` performs exactly one rounding, ever. The two are the same number for the first few steps and then they are not, and after that they never agree again.

Read the two figures the run prints. The step at which they stop being **the same float** arrives almost immediately, in single digits. The magnitude of the disagreement after two hundred thousand steps is around forty nanoseconds, which sounds like nothing and is nothing, physically.

It is not nothing for a checksum. A replay that recomputes its clock the other way produces a different number for the same instant, and if the clock feeds anything at all, a controller period, a sensor trigger, a logging condition, the two runs diverge for a reason nobody would look for. Store the integer `steps` as the truth and derive the time from it: integers do not drift.

lessons.title: The Fingerprint of a Run
lessons.goal: Reduce a whole trajectory to one hash so two runs can be compared in a single line.
lessons.theory:
Comparing two runs by eye does not scale past ten steps. Comparing them element by element works but produces nothing you can put in a log line or a test assertion. What you want is a **checksum**: one short string that changes if anything at all changed.

The recipe is fixed and the details matter. Pack each number into its exact binary form with `struct.pack` using an explicit byte order, here `<d` for a little endian double. Do not format it as text, because printing rounds and two different floats can print the same. Then feed the bytes to a cryptographic hash, `hashlib.sha256`, and keep a prefix of the hexadecimal digest.

Use `hashlib`, not the built in `hash`. Python randomises the hash of strings and bytes per process by default, so the built in one is a different function on every run and would make this lesson print a different answer each time. That is the exact failure this chapter is about, hiding inside the tool you reached for to detect it.

With this in hand a determinism test is one comparison, a regression test on a physics change is one string, and a bug report carries a fingerprint the person on the other end can check in a second.

lessons.title: Where Two Runs Split
lessons.goal: Perturb a chaotic run by one unit in the last place and find the step at which it becomes a different run.
lessons.theory:
Determinism is worth this much effort because the systems worth simulating amplify differences. A contact rich scene is **chaotic** in the technical sense: two states that differ by the smallest amount a double can express end up nowhere near each other.

The rig below is a Sinai billiard, a body bouncing inside a square box with a round obstacle at the centre. It has no randomness whatsoever, only reflections. `math.nextafter(X0, 1.0)` returns the very next representable float above the starting position, so the two runs begin 2,8 times 10 to the minus 17 metres apart, which is a fifty thousandth of a proton diameter.

Read the step at which the separation crosses `THRESHOLD` at one millimetre, and the separation at the end. The initial difference is amplified by roughly fourteen orders of magnitude, and after that the two simulations are not approximations of each other, they are different runs.

That is the argument in full. It is not that a non reproducible simulator is untidy, it is that the difference between reproducible and not is the difference between a run you can debug and a run whose result is a single sample from a distribution you never characterised.

        r = math.hypot(dx, dy)
        if 0.0 < r < OBSTACLE:
            nx, ny = dx / r, dy / r
            dot = vx * nx + vy * ny
            vx = vx - 2.0 * dot * nx
            vy = vy - 2.0 * dot * ny
            x, y = 0.5 + nx * OBSTACLE, 0.5 + ny * OBSTACLE
        trace.append((x, y))
    return trace

lessons.title: Counting in Whole Numbers
lessons.goal: Represent positions as scaled integers and show the sum becomes independent of the order.
lessons.theory:
There is a way to make the arithmetic exactly reproducible rather than merely carefully ordered: stop using floats. **Fixed point** stores a quantity as an integer number of units, with the unit fixed by a `SCALE`. At a scale of a million, positions are counted in micrometres and Python's integers are exact and unbounded.

Integer addition is associative and commutative, so a fixed point sum does not care what order it is given the terms in. The run below sums the same positions forwards and backwards in both representations, and the two differences it prints are the whole lesson: one is a small number, the other is a hard zero.

This is what lockstep networked simulations do, the ones where every machine has to agree on the state without exchanging it. It is also what a safety case sometimes demands, because a fixed point run is reproducible across compilers, architectures and optimisation levels, which floats are not.

The costs are real. You lose dynamic range, so a scale that resolves micrometres overflows into slow big integers if the world is large enough. You have to write your own square root and trigonometry. And every conversion at the boundary rounds. It is the right answer for a small deterministic core, not for a whole engine.

lessons.title: The Machine on the Other Desk
lessons.goal: Show that two expressions of the same mathematics disagree in the last bits and pin the one you meant.
lessons.theory:
A run can be reproducible on your machine and not on the next one, and the reason is usually that two spellings of the same formula are not the same computation.

`math.fsum` sums exactly and rounds once; a plain loop rounds at every term. `math.hypot(dx, dy)` is computed to be accurate and to avoid overflow; `math.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)` is three operations with three roundings. Both members of each pair are correct implementations of the same mathematics, and they return different floats.

The same thing happens without you writing anything different. A compiler that contracts a multiply and an add into a fused instruction, a library that dispatches to a vector unit on one machine and not another, a build with fast math enabled: each of those silently swaps one member of a pair like these for the other, and the run stops matching the run on the machine next to you.

So the rule is to pin the arithmetic the way you pin the seed. Choose the spelling deliberately, write it once behind a helper, and treat a change of expression as a change to the model that invalidates every stored checksum. The two numbers below are small. Lesson sm6-6 already showed what a small number becomes.
