lessons.title: The Harness That Refuses
lessons.goal: Build a determinism test that runs a world twice and reports the first step where the two disagree.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter becomes a rule you can enforce, and the enforcement is fifteen lines.

The harness takes a **builder**, a function that constructs and runs a world from scratch, calls it twice, and compares the two traces sample by sample. It returns the index of the first disagreement, or minus one when there is none. That index is the most valuable number in the report: it tells you where to look, and the state one step earlier is the smallest reproduction of the bug.

Run it in continuous integration on every change to the physics. It catches the whole family at once: an unseeded generator, an iteration over an unordered container, a cached value that survives between runs, a thread that finishes in a different order. None of those are visible by reading the code, and all of them show up here as an index.

The two builders below are the same world. `careful` seeds from a constant. `sloppy` seeds from a module level counter that advances on every call, which is a fair model of a real defect: a generator created once at import time and shared, an object identity used as a key, a cache that was warm the second time. It is fully deterministic as a program, which is why this page prints the same numbers every time, and it is not deterministic as a simulator, which is exactly what the harness is there to say out loud.
lessons.task: Fill in `first_divergence` so it reports the index of the first differing sample, and read the verdict for both builders.

lessons.title: The Motor That Answers Instantly
lessons.goal: Add a first order lag to the actuator and measure the distance the instant model over promises.
lessons.theory:
The most common lie a simulator tells is that a commanded velocity is the velocity. You write `v = command` because it is one line and because the alternative needs a parameter you do not have, and from then on the model has an actuator with infinite bandwidth.

Real drives take time. A geared brushed motor under a velocity loop behaves close to a first order lag, `v = v + (COMMAND - v) * (DT / tau)`, where `tau` is the time to cover 63 percent of a step change. For a small robot drive with a current loop underneath it, `tau` sits between 30 and 150 milliseconds; for a large arm joint under gravity it can be half a second.

That missing `tau` does not average out. Over a single one second move the instant model always arrives further along than the real machine, by roughly `tau` times the commanded speed, and the error is in the same direction every time. Systematic errors do not cancel over a mission, they add up.

The run below drives the same one second command through the instant model and through three lags, and prints the distance and the percentage. Do not read this as an argument for always adding a lag. Read it as a price list: this is what an unmodelled `tau` costs, so you can decide whether your question can afford it.

lessons.goal: Measure how far a trajectory drifts when the modelled mass is wrong by a fixed percentage.
lessons.theory:
Every parameter in your model is a measurement, and every measurement has an error. A robot mass taken from a bill of materials is out by whatever the cables, the fasteners and the payload weigh. Fifteen percent is a normal miss for a machine nobody has put on a scale.

The damage is not proportional to time, it is worse than that. A force applied to the wrong mass gives the wrong acceleration, which integrates twice into position, so the gap grows with the square of the elapsed time. That is why a model that looks perfectly acceptable over half a second is useless over ten.

The run below applies the same force profile to the nominal mass and to one `MASS_ERROR` heavier, then prints the divergence at four instants. The numbers are what makes the choice concrete: if your question is what happens in the next 200 milliseconds, a fifteen percent mass error is nothing; if it is where the robot ends up after a ten second manoeuvre, it is centimetres.

This is also the cheapest thing to fix in a real project. Put the robot on a scale, weigh the payload, and one number that was a guess becomes a measurement.

lessons.title: The Sensor That Rounds
lessons.goal: Quantise a position into encoder ticks and measure the noise it injects into the velocity estimate.
lessons.theory:
Inside the simulator a position is a double with sixteen digits. On the robot, that position is whatever the encoder can express, and nothing finer exists.

A 1024 count encoder on a 40 millimetre wheel resolves `2 * pi * WHEEL_RADIUS / TICKS_PER_REV`, which is a quarter of a millimetre. A controller reading raw floats out of a simulator has been handed information the hardware does not have, and every result derived from it is optimistic.

The position error is bounded and small, and on its own it would not matter. What matters is what happens when you differentiate. A velocity estimated as the change in position over `DT` divides a quarter millimetre step by two milliseconds, which is 0,12 metres per second of noise on a signal whose true value is 1. Differentiation multiplies quantisation by one over the timestep, and a faster loop makes it worse rather than better.

That is why the same estimator that looks clean in an unquantised simulator is unusable on hardware, and why a simulator that does not model the sensor cannot be used to choose a filter. Read the two figures: the position error is a quarter of a millimetre, and the velocity error is around a tenth of the signal it is meant to measure.

lessons.title: One Step Late
lessons.goal: Delay the command path through a queue and measure how far the trajectory moves.
lessons.theory:
Between a command leaving your loop and the wheel feeling it there is a serial link, a driver buffer, a firmware loop running at its own rate and a current controller. Each adds delay, and the total is usually several milliseconds and sometimes tens.

The simulator applies the command in the step it was issued. That difference has a name, **latency**, and it is modelled with the simplest structure there is: a queue of fixed length. Push the new command in, pop the one that has waited long enough, apply that.

The measurement below is deliberately open loop, the same fixed command profile in every run, so what you are reading is the delay's effect on the **model** and nothing else. That separation matters: latency inside a feedback loop also changes stability, and mixing the two makes it impossible to say which effect you measured.

Read the trajectory gap. Against a smoothly varying command a few steps of delay barely moves the path; against a sharply changing one it moves it by a large fraction of the amplitude. So the honest statement about latency is never a single number, it is a number attached to a command bandwidth.
lessons.task: Push each command into the queue and apply the one that comes out, then read the trajectory gap at each latency.
lessons.hint: `queue.append` puts the fresh command at the back and `queue.pop(0)` takes the oldest from the front.

lessons.title: The Floor That Is Not Flat
lessons.goal: Add a ripple to the ground and measure the normal force it removes at speed.
lessons.theory:
A floor in a simulator is a plane. A real workshop floor has a texture, a warehouse floor has expansion joints, and a paved outdoor surface has a ripple of a few millimetres with a wavelength of a few centimetres.

Amplitude alone says nothing. What a wheel feels is the vertical acceleration needed to follow the profile, and that acceleration is the amplitude times the square of the angular frequency, `RIPPLE * omega * omega`, with `omega` equal to `2 * pi * speed / PITCH`. Speed enters squared, so the same 3 millimetre ripple is nothing at walking pace and violent at a metre per second.

The consequence is the number that matters to a contact model. The normal force is `MASS * (G + accel)`, and when the required downward acceleration exceeds gravity the force would have to be negative, which a floor cannot do. The wheel leaves the ground. While it is airborne there is no normal force, and lesson sm5-1 established that no normal force means **no friction**: no traction, no braking, no steering authority.

A flat floor model reports a robot that is always in contact and always has grip. Read the airborne fraction at one metre per second and decide whether the plane was a fair model of your floor.

lessons.title: Randomising the Room
lessons.goal: Sample the uncertain parameters over their ranges and report the distribution of outcomes instead of one number.
lessons.theory:
The previous lessons each measured one gap with one wrong value. In practice you do not know any of the values, you know a range, and the honest output of a simulator is not a number but a **distribution**.

**Domain randomisation** is the technique: draw each uncertain parameter from its plausible range on every rollout, run hundreds of rollouts, and report what came out. The parameters here are the mass, the actuator time constant and the rolling resistance, each drawn with `rng.uniform` between the bounds a real project would get from a scale, a step response and a coast down test.

What you report from it decides whether the simulator was useful. The mean is the least interesting figure. The **worst case** and the **fraction outside tolerance** are the ones a decision needs, because an average inside the tolerance says nothing about how often the tolerance is missed. Read those two rows before the mean.

The generator is seeded, so this page prints the same distribution every time. That is not decoration: an unseeded randomisation study cannot be compared against the study you ran last week, which makes the whole exercise unfalsifiable. Randomise the model, never the run.

CRR_LOW = 0.010
CRR_HIGH = 0.030

lessons.title: Fitting the Mirror to the Log
lessons.goal: Recover an actuator time constant from a logged step response by minimising the squared residual.
lessons.theory:
So far the parameters arrived from outside. The other direction is more useful: run the real machine once, record what it did, and fit the model to it.

The procedure is the simplest optimisation there is. Sweep the parameter over a plausible range, run the model at each value, sum the squared differences against the log, and keep the value with the smallest sum. For one parameter with a smooth response a sweep is fine and it has the advantage that you see the whole curve rather than the point some solver stopped at.

The residual you keep matters as much as the parameter. A residual near zero says the model can reproduce the data, and a residual that stays stubbornly high says something in the machine is not in your model at all. The next lesson is entirely about that second case.

The log below is generated inside the program from `TRUE_TAU`, so the fit can be checked against the answer. On a real bench you do not get that, and the parameter you recover is only as good as how much the manoeuvre excited it: a step is enough for a time constant, and a constant speed command tells you nothing about one at all.
lessons.task: Compute the squared residual of each candidate and keep the `tau` with the smallest one, then compare it against `TRUE_TAU`.
lessons.hint: Sum the squared difference between model and log at every sample, and keep the candidate when the sum beats the best so far.

COMMAND = 1.0
TRUE_TAU = 0.17

    out = []
    for _ in range(STEPS):
        v = v + (COMMAND - v) * (DT / tau)
        out.append(v)
    return out

best_tau = 0.0
best_error = 1e18
candidate = 0.02
while candidate < 0.5:

    candidate = candidate + 0.001

print("residual", "%.3e" % best_error)

lessons.title: What the Fit Cannot Remove
lessons.goal: Show that a good fit of the wrong model leaves a residual no parameter value can reduce.
lessons.theory:
A fitted parameter is not a validated model. If the real machine has a mechanism your model does not have, the fit will still return a number, and it will return the number that hides the missing mechanism best.

The log here comes from a plant with a time constant **and** four steps of transport delay. Fitting only the time constant, the sweep has nowhere to put the delay, so it compensates by choosing a slower `tau` than the truth and stops at a residual it cannot get below. That biased parameter is the dangerous part: it looks like a measurement and it is a fudge factor carrying the error of a mechanism you did not model.

Searching both together tells a different story. The residual collapses by orders of magnitude and the recovered time constant lands on the truth. The size of the drop is the evidence that the second mechanism is real and not a curve fitting artefact.

The habit worth taking from this is simple. Always look at the residual, never only at the parameter. A residual that will not go down, or one whose shape follows the input rather than looking like noise, is the model telling you it is missing something, and no amount of tuning what you already have will answer it.

lessons.title: The Error Budget
lessons.goal: Combine the measured modelling gaps into one honest tolerance for the simulator's answer.
lessons.theory:
Every lesson in this chapter measured one gap. A report needs one number, and the way to get from several to one is an **error budget**.

There are two ways to add the contributions and the difference between them is not cosmetic. The **worst case** is the plain sum, which assumes every error is at its maximum and all in the same direction at the same time. The **quadrature** sum is the square root of the sum of the squares, `math.sqrt(sum(c * c for c in contributions))`, which is the right combination for contributions that are independent and can point either way.

Use the plain sum for anything with a hard limit, a clearance, a joint stop, a safety envelope, because a collision does not care that the alignment was unlikely. Use quadrature for a typical accuracy figure. Quoting the quadrature figure as a guarantee is the error that gets robots stuck in doorways.

The four contributions are recomputed on the same one second manoeuvre. The mass error enters through the time constant, because for a first order velocity plant `tau` is the mass over the damping, so a body ten percent heavier answers ten percent more slowly. The run prints both totals. Then it says the sentence the simulator is actually entitled to say: this model predicts the position after one second to within so many centimetres, and here is the largest single reason why.
lessons.task: Add up the contributions both ways and print which one is the largest single term.
lessons.hint: `sum` gives the worst case, and the quadrature figure is the square root of the sum of the squares.

lessons.title: Writing the Trace
lessons.goal: Record one row per step to a CSV file and read it back without losing a digit.
lessons.theory:
The first thing a simulator has to be able to do after running is say what happened. A **trace** is one row per step: the step index, the simulated time and the state.

Write it with the `csv` module rather than by hand. It handles the quoting, the line endings and the reader, and the reader is the half people forget: a log you cannot parse back is a log you cannot compare against the next run.

Write the floats with `str`, which in Python 3 gives the shortest text that reads back as the **same** float. Do not format them to a fixed number of decimals here. The recording is the reference the rest of this chapter is checked against, so any rounding at this stage is an error you can never remove later, and lesson sm8-5 measures what that rounding costs.

Open the file with `newline=""`, which is what the csv module requires to avoid blank rows between records on some platforms, and delete it when the run is done. A simulator that leaves files behind in whatever directory it was started from is a simulator nobody can run twice in the same place.

lessons.title: Inputs Are Smaller Than States
lessons.goal: Record the command tape instead of the state trace and measure how much smaller it is.
lessons.theory:
A state trace grows with the number of bodies times the number of steps. A minute of a modest scene at 500 Hz is millions of numbers, and most of them are the deterministic consequence of a handful of decisions.

So record the **decisions**. The input tape holds only what entered the simulation from outside: commands, spawns, disturbances. Everything else is recomputed by running the simulator again, which chapter six made possible by making the recomputation exact.

Squeeze it further by recording only **changes**. A command that stays at 0,4 for two hundred steps is one entry with a step index, not two hundred entries, and real robot commands are piecewise constant far more often than they are not.

The run below counts both. The state trace is two floats per step for one body; the tape is one pair per change. That ratio is why a bug report can be an attachment of a few hundred bytes instead of a file nobody will download, and it is why replay based debugging is the normal way large simulations are shipped.

lessons.title: Replay From the Tape
lessons.goal: Rebuild a run from its seed and its tape and prove the trajectory is identical by checksum.
lessons.theory:
A tape is only a recording if something can play it. The player walks the steps, applies the entries whose index has arrived, and runs the same physics as the original.

The pointer pattern is the whole of it. Keep an index into the tape, and at each step consume every entry whose step number equals the current one, updating the command in force. Consume in a `while`, not an `if`: two entries can land on the same step and an `if` silently drops the second.

The proof that it worked is the checksum from lesson sm6-5. Not a plot, not a final position, the whole trajectory reduced to one string. If the two strings match, the replay is the original run in every bit, and any tool that works on one works on the other.

That equality is what makes the technique worth the trouble. A recorded run can be replayed under a debugger, replayed with extra logging switched on, replayed at a different speed, replayed a thousand times, and it is the same run every time. Without chapter six none of that is true and a tape is just a hint about what might have happened.

lessons.title: Snapshots and Seeking
lessons.goal: Store periodic snapshots so any step can be reached by re simulating only the remainder.
lessons.theory:
Replaying from the start is fine for a two second run and hopeless for a twenty minute one. Jumping to step 118.400 to look at a contact means eighteen minutes of simulation before you can look at anything.

The cure is a **snapshot** every `SNAPSHOT_EVERY` steps: the complete state, enough to continue from. Seeking to a target then means loading the last snapshot at or before it, `(target // SNAPSHOT_EVERY) * SNAPSHOT_EVERY`, and re simulating the remainder, which is at most one snapshot interval.

The interval is the knob and it trades memory against seek time in the obvious way. Video codecs solve the same problem with the same structure and call them key frames.

The test that matters is not that seeking is fast, it is that the state you land on is **the same state** the full run had at that step. That has to be asserted, not assumed: a snapshot that forgot one field, the accumulator, the tape pointer, the generator state, produces a run that continues plausibly and wrongly. Read the difference column: it has to be a hard zero and not merely small.
lessons.task: Find the snapshot at or before the target and the number of steps left to re simulate, then check the result against the full run.
lessons.hint: Integer division by the interval and back gives the snapshot index; what remains is the target minus that.

lessons.title: Floats That Survive the Trip
lessons.goal: Compare an exact JSON round trip against a formatted one and measure the error the formatting adds.
lessons.theory:
A snapshot is worthless if writing it out and reading it back changes it. Chapter six spent nine lessons on differences in the last bit; a serialiser that rounds to three decimals throws away forty of them.

Python's `json.dumps` writes floats with `repr`, which produces the shortest decimal string that reads back as **exactly** the same double. So `json.loads(json.dumps(state))` is an identity on floats, and the error column for it is a hard zero rather than a small number.

Formatting with `"%.3f"` is the alternative people reach for because the file looks tidier. It costs about half a millimetre per value at metre scale, which sounds harmless until you remember lesson sm6-6, where a difference of 10 to the minus 17 became 20 centimetres.

So the rule for anything a replay will read: write the exact representation, and keep the pretty formatting for the report a human reads. If you need the file to be smaller, use a binary format like `struct`, which is both exact and shorter than the text, and never buy space with digits.

lessons.title: Recording Less, Guessing Between
lessons.goal: Store every nth sample and reconstruct the rest by interpolation, measuring what the gap costs.
lessons.theory:
Between recording everything and recording only the inputs there is a middle road: record every `keep`th sample and rebuild the rest by interpolation. It is what a telemetry link does when it cannot carry the full rate.

The reconstruction is the same blend as lesson sm2-3, and so is the error term: a straight line through a curve is wrong by roughly the second derivative times the square of the gap. Doubling the gap quadruples the error, which is a much better trade than it sounds, because the storage falls in direct proportion.

What this cannot be used for is replay. An interpolated state is not a state the simulator ever had, so continuing from it produces a different run, and lesson sm6-6 says how different. Decimated traces are for looking at, for plots and for reports.

Read the table as a price list. It tells you what a given storage budget costs in reconstruction accuracy for this trajectory, and the answer is specific to how curved the trajectory is: the same decimation on a smooth coast is free and on a bouncing contact is worthless.

lessons.title: A Bug Report Is a Seed and a Tape
lessons.goal: Serialise a failing run as a seed and an input tape and reproduce the failure from the text.
lessons.theory:
The most useful thing a simulator can hand a colleague is not a description of a failure, it is the failure itself.

A reproduction is a small document: the `SEED`, the timestep, and the tape. Nothing else, because everything else is derived. Written as JSON it is a few hundred characters, it goes in a ticket, and the person who opens it gets the identical run rather than an approximation of your description.

The run below drives a rover along a corridor from a generated tape, detects the failure, which here is leaving the safe corridor at `LIMIT`, writes the report, loads it back and reproduces the same failure at the same step. Those two step numbers being equal is the whole claim, and it is printed rather than asserted so you can see it.

One discipline makes this work: the report has to be generated by the **failing** run, automatically, at the moment of failure. A report reconstructed afterwards from what you remember doing is a description again, and the failures worth reporting are exactly the ones you cannot remember your way back into.

lessons.title: Shrinking the Tape
lessons.goal: Reduce a failing tape to a minimal one by removing entries that the failure does not need.
lessons.theory:
A recorded failure is reproducible and usually far larger than the bug. Nine hundred steps and thirty commands, of which two matter.

**Delta debugging** shrinks it mechanically. Walk the entries, try the tape without each one, and if the failure still reproduces, keep the shorter tape and carry on. lessons.title: The Playback That Notices
lessons.goal: Compare a replay against its recorded checksums step by step and report the first divergence.
lessons.theory:
A replay that silently produces a different run is worse than no replay at all, because you will read its output believing it is the recorded one.

So record a checksum per step next to the tape, and have the player compare as it goes. The moment the live value differs from the recorded one, stop and report the index. That index is the same gift as in lesson sm6-9: the step before it is the last state both runs agreed on, and whatever the player did at that step is the bug.

The causes are always the same short list. The physics changed since the recording, a constant was retuned, the timestep moved, a library version brought different rounding, or the recording was made before a fix. lessons.goal: Resolve the rover against the four walls of the room with positional correction and restitution.
lessons.theory:
The room is four half spaces, written as a unit normal and an offset exactly as in lesson sm3-1. The left wall is normal `(1, 0)` at offset 0, the right wall is normal `(-1, 0)` at offset -4, and the two horizontal walls follow the same pattern.

The signed distance from the rover centre is `nx * body.x + ny * body.y - offset`, so the penetration is the radius minus that distance. One routine handles all four walls and any wall you add later at any angle, which is the entire reason for representing them this way instead of as four separate comparisons on coordinates.

The response is chapter four in two parts. Push out along the normal by the depth beyond `SLOP`, then reflect the normal component of the velocity with `RESTITUTION`. Take the normal component with a dot product, `body.vx * nx + body.vy * ny`, and only reflect it when it is negative: a body already moving away is not approaching the wall, and reflecting it again is how a body gets stuck vibrating in a corner.

The invariant to check afterwards is the one from lesson sm2-8. When the run ends, no body is outside the room by more than the `SLOP` the solver was told to forgive. The last rows measure that instead of assuming it.

lessons.title: The Floor and the Air
lessons.goal: Add rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag to the rover and measure the coasting distance each removes.
lessons.theory:
The rover coasts forever unless something takes the energy back. Two mechanisms from chapter five do it, and they act at completely different speeds.

**Rolling resistance** is constant in magnitude, `CRR * G` as a deceleration, opposing the motion. It dominates at low speed and it is the only one of the two that brings the rover to a genuine stop, at the distance the closed form of lesson sm5-7 predicts.

**Aerodynamic drag** is quadratic, `0.5 * RHO * CD * AREA * speed * speed / MASS` as a deceleration. At 0,3 metres per second it is negligible; at 3 metres per second it is the larger of the two. A rover simulated with drag alone will coast for an implausibly long tail, and one simulated with rolling resistance alone will overstate its top speed.

Read the four rows. Rolling alone lands on its closed form, which is the check that the integration is right. Drag alone travels much further because it never finishes. Both together is shorter than either, and the difference between that number and the rolling only number is exactly what the air was worth on this manoeuvre.
lessons.task: Write the two deceleration terms and read the coasting distance for each combination against the closed form.
lessons.hint: The rolling term is constant and carries the sign of the motion, the drag term goes with the speed squared.

    speed = v0

lessons.title: The Beam and Its Lies
lessons.goal: Cast a range beam against the room walls and add the quantisation and noise a real sensor has.
lessons.theory:
The rover needs to see, and a range sensor in a simulator is the ray cast of lesson sm3-5 aimed at the walls of lesson sm9-2.

Against a plane the intersection is one division. The signed distance to the wall is `nx * x + ny * y - offset` and the rate at which the ray closes on it is the dot product of the direction with the normal. When that rate is negative the ray is approaching, and the distance along the ray is the first divided by minus the second. The reading is the smallest positive one across the four walls, capped at `MAX_RANGE`.

That number is the truth, and no sensor returns the truth. Chapter seven measured why: the device reports in steps of its `RESOLUTION`, and it has noise. Both go on afterwards, in that order, with `round(true_range / RESOLUTION) * RESOLUTION` and then a draw from the world's own seeded generator.

The noise has to come from `world.rng` and not from a fresh generator or the module level one, or lesson sm6-1 happens to a project that is otherwise deterministic. Read the last row: the reading a controller would act on is a couple of centimetres from the geometry, every time, in a direction you cannot predict but can reproduce.
lessons.task: Quantise the true range to the sensor resolution and add the seeded noise, then read the error the model injects.

lessons.title: The Mission on One Page
lessons.goal: Serialise the whole mission as a seed and a tape and reproduce its fingerprint from the text.
lessons.theory:
The mission is now a document. A seed, a timestep, a step count and a tape of commands, in JSON, a few hundred characters.

Everything else is a consequence: the trajectory, the contacts, the sensor readings, the fingerprint. That is the payoff of the whole course and it only works because every previous property holds at once. Fixed timestep from chapter two, a canonical order from chapter six, a seeded generator on the world, exact float text from lesson sm8-5.

The test is not that the replay looks similar. It is that the fingerprint of the replay, computed from the reloaded text, equals the fingerprint of the live run. One string against one string, printed so you can see them.

When it holds you can do things that are otherwise impossible: attach a failure to a ticket, bisect a regression across a hundred commits by replaying the same tape, run the same mission on a colleague's machine, or store a thousand missions as a few hundred kilobytes and re run all of them nightly.
lessons.task: Build the mission dictionary, write it and read it back, then compare the fingerprint of the replay against the live one.
lessons.hint: Three keys and the tape, `json.dumps` to text, `json.loads` to get it back, then run the replay from what came back.

lessons.title: The Report the Mirror Owes You
lessons.goal: Run the same mission against a degraded model and publish the simulator's answer with its tolerance.
lessons.theory:
The last thing a simulator produces is not a trajectory, it is a **claim with a tolerance on it**. This lesson builds that claim from measurements the model made about itself.

The same mission runs five times. Once on the honest model, then once for each modelling gap taken on its own: the actuator lag of lesson sm7-1, the transport latency of sm7-4, the mass error of sm7-2 and the sensor resolution of sm7-3. Each run reports the distance it ended from the honest one, and those four numbers are the error budget of lesson sm7-9.

Combine them both ways. The quadrature figure is the accuracy to quote; the worst case sum is the one to design clearances against. Print both and say which term dominates, because that term is the only one worth spending an afternoon measuring on the real machine.

That is the end of the course. The simulator you have built runs on a timestep you chose deliberately, detects and resolves contact, has friction that stops things, reproduces itself bit for bit, can be recorded and replayed from a few hundred characters, and knows how far from the truth it sits. The last property is the one that makes the other five worth anything.
lessons.task: Total the four measured gaps both ways and name the dominant term, then read the tolerance the mission is entitled to claim.
lessons.hint: The plain sum is the worst case and the quadrature is the square root of the sum of the squares.
